tagline: Waterfalls and river overlooks shaped the course of this early scenic highway.
intro: The Historic Columbia River Highway winds through the Gorge from the damp Sandy River country to dry oak savannahs near The Dalles. Oregon’s transportation department describes a narrow, winding 70-mile byway and recommends three to five hours for the drive. The Federal Highway Administration lists it as an All-American Road, highlighting river overlooks, waterfalls and spring wildflowers.

Sam Hill and engineer Samuel C. Lancaster promoted a road modeled on Europe’s scenic highways. Construction began in 1913, with Lancaster arranging the route to reach waterfalls and viewpoints. Bridges and viaducts carried the road across streams and along steep hillsides; masonry retaining walls supported the highway, while guard walls protected its edges. The highway became part of U.S. 30 in 1926, but later bypasses displaced the original road. Some surviving sections now form the Historic Columbia River Highway State Trail for nonmotorized travel.

From Troutdale, follow the Sandy River before climbing through Springdale and Corbett to Crown Point. Lancaster’s loops descend 600 feet toward a succession of waterfalls, including Multnomah and Horsetail. At Dodson the byway joins I-84, continuing through Hood River before the historic road resumes at Mosier. The eastern leg reaches Rowena Crest, then descends through the Rowena Loops toward The Dalles.
notice: Look for the highway’s stone guard walls and arches.

moments.title: Vista House, Crown Point
moments.text: Vista House gives a roadside comfort station an octagonal stone form, with gray sandstone walls and a green tile roof. Architect Edgar M. Lazarus designed it in the Art Nouveau style; it was completed in 1918 on a promontory 733 feet above the Columbia. Lancaster proposed the observatory and its name, and a group of Portland civic and business leaders raised funds. Their subscriptions fell short, leaving Multnomah County to pay most of the construction cost. Marble finishes extend even into the toilets. A five-year restoration ended in 2005, with a rebuilt roof and repairs and replacements to the interior finishes.
moments.notice: Gray sandstone walls, a green tile roof and an octagonal plan distinguish Vista House.

moments.title: Horsetail Falls
moments.text: Horsetail Falls takes its name from the shape of the water against a rounded rockface. Horsetail Creek drops over columnar basalt beside the Historic Columbia River Highway, within the road’s waterfall corridor. The bridge here dates to 1914: a 60-foot span made of reinforced concrete. In 1998 it was strengthened with fibre-reinforced plastic, a later addition to the original structure. Farther up the creek is a second waterfall, known as Upper Horsetail or Ponytail Falls, reached by a footpath. That path passes steep cliffs; the Forest Service urges caution on the trails, a distinction from the roadside view.
moments.notice: The water and rounded rockface give Horsetail Falls its namesake shape.

moments.title: Rowena Loops
moments.text: Eastbound from Mosier, the historic road reaches Rowena Crest before descending a series of horseshoe curves to Rowena. State highway engineer J. H. Scott laid out this final section toward The Dalles, using existing county roads for the climb. A completion ceremony followed near Rowena in June 1922, when highway promoter Simon Benson symbolically helped pave the final portion. The curves lie within Mayer State Park, with an overlook at the crest and the dry eastern Columbia River plateau beyond Mosier. Below the loops, the route picked up an earlier Oregon-Washington Railroad and Navigation Company alignment toward The Dalles.
